data.sourcePassage:
Decomposition is the first pillar of computational thinking. It means breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems. Think of building a house: no one tries to build the whole thing in a single step. Instead, the project is split into foundations, walls, roof, windows, and decoration. Each part can be handled by a specialist and tested independently before being combined.

In computing, decomposition leads directly to modular design. A programmer writing a school library system does not write one enormous block of code. Instead, they create separate modules: one for storing book details, one for searching, one for recording loans, and one for flagging overdue books. Each module can be written and tested on its own. If a bug appears, only the faulty module needs fixing. If a new feature is needed, a new module can be added without disturbing the others.

Decomposition also allows teams to work in parallel. Different programmers tackle different sub-problems at the same time, significantly reducing how long a large project takes.

data.sourcePassage:
Abstraction is the second pillar of computational thinking. It means removing irrelevant detail from a model or system so that only the information needed for the task at hand remains. The key insight is that you do not need to understand every detail of a system to use it effectively.

Consider a map. The real world contains textured roads, three-dimensional buildings, changing weather, and thousands of people moving around. A navigation map abstracts all of that away. It shows roads as lines, buildings as rectangles, and ignores people entirely. The detail it keeps — road connections, distances, and landmarks — is exactly what a traveller needs. The detail it removes would only cause confusion.

In programming, variables are a powerful form of abstraction. When a programmer writes playerScore = 10, they are storing a value without needing to know its binary representation or memory address. Similarly, when a programmer calls calculateTax(income), they use the function without knowing how the tax calculation works internally. The function's name, inputs, and output form its interface — the only part other programmers need to understand. The internal logic is abstracted away. This makes large programs much easier to build and maintain.

questions.question: Explain how using variables in a program is an example of abstraction.
questions.modelAnswer: A variable name such as playerScore abstracts away the binary memory address and binary representation of the stored value. The programmer can read and update the value using a meaningful name without needing to know where it is stored in memory or how it is represented in binary. This allows the programmer to think about game logic rather than hardware details.

data.sourcePassage:
Decomposition and abstraction are always used together in software development. Consider building a quiz application. First, decomposition splits the project into sub-problems: load questions, display a question, accept a user answer, check correctness, update the score, and show final results. Each sub-problem becomes a subroutine.

Then abstraction is applied within each subroutine. The loadQuestions() module hides how it reads and parses a file — the rest of the program simply receives a list of questions. The displayQuestion() module hides how it renders text on screen — the rest of the program just calls it with a question object. The checkAnswer() module hides the comparison logic — the rest of the program only sees the result.

The outcome is a program built from clean, independent modules. Each module does one job, has a clear interface, and hides unnecessary detail from the rest of the system. If the file format changes, only loadQuestions() needs updating. If the screen layout changes, only displayQuestion() needs updating. Programmers can work on different modules simultaneously because each module's interface — not its implementation — is all that matters to the others. This combination of decomposition and abstraction is the foundation of all professional software development.

questions.question: Explain the difference between decomposition and abstraction, and describe how they are used together in the quiz application example from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Decomposition divides the quiz application into separate sub-problems: load questions, display question, accept answer, check correctness, update score, show results. Each becomes a subroutine. Abstraction is then applied inside each subroutine: each module hides its internal logic and exposes only its interface. For example, loadQuestions() hides file-reading details and just provides a list; checkAnswer() hides comparison logic and returns a result. Together, decomposition creates independent units of work and abstraction keeps each unit's implementation hidden, making the program easier to build, maintain, and extend.
